youtube_description:
On an early-autumn day in 1594, a crowd gathered on the Sanjo riverbank in Kyoto to watch a thief put to death in a cauldron. The records give us a name, a crime and a punishment. The legend gave us a Robin Hood, an assassin of Hideyoshi, a poet and a father. Which parts of Ishikawa Goemon are history, and which were lent by the storytellers? Follow time-travelling reporter Tokio Kamiya as he files a dispatch from Kyoto, 1594.

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

scenes.narration: Let me start with what is solid. I carry the surviving records in my notebook. Tonight a court noble, Yamashina Tokitsune, will write in his diary that thieves were boiled in a cauldron by the Sanjo bridge, and nineteen of their band crucified. He names no one. A Spanish merchant will later describe the same scene, and a Jesuit's note beside his account gives the name: Ishikawa Goemon. That is nearly all they give. No poor villagers are fed. No castle is entered. Everything else has to be weighed against those few dry lines.

scenes.narration: Who was he? I cannot tell you. Several provinces claim him as a native son, and the records do not choose between them. The stories say he trained as a ninja under a famous master in Iga, and served a lord before turning to crime. I find no document for any of it. The earliest tales I know of were written long after his death. I think that is the first thing to understand about Goemon: his birth is a blank, and the storytellers have been filling it ever since.

I think a thief in a cauldron deserves one honest sentence: a man named Ishikawa Goemon was executed in Kyoto in 1594, and a great many people have wanted him to be more.
